claim: A 7B model can be trained or fine-tuned on a single 16 GB consumer card at 70% MFU using an 8-bit training pipeline with selective recomputation, optimizer offload and chunked logits/attention workspace, and a 32B model trains on 4x RTX 4090 at 3,400 tokens/s and 51% MFU.
stance_target: the claim that a 7B-total model fits on 64 GB cards; LLMQ shows it fits on 16 GB, so the memory constraint is not the binding one
scope_conditions: single RTX 5060Ti 16 GB and 4x RTX 4090 24 GB; FP8/BF16 training with ZeRO-1 optimizer sharding; no algorithmic approximations
quoted_support: LLMQ is able to train or fine-tune a 7B model on a single 16GB mid-range gaming card, or a 32B model on a workstation equipped with 4 RTX 4090s... Even on a constrained 16GB RTX 5060Ti, the system enables 7B model pretraining with a remarkable 70% MFU.

claim: On recent consumer GPUs the cards cannot communicate directly with each other over PCIe, so placing sharded weights in host memory actually REDUCES the communication required during forward and backward passes, because the host copy is reused across the backward pass and all gradient-accumulation forwards.
stance_target: the repo's claim that the no-P2P fabric changes which parallelism strategy is optimal, and specifically that host-resident weights are cheaper than GPU-resident sharded weights here
scope_conditions: consumer GPUs with PCIe P2P disabled; multi-GPU single node; weights sharded across workers
quoted_support: As recent generation gaming GPUs are unable to communicate directly with each other over PCIe, we found that offloading sharded parameters fully to the CPU does not increase the communication required during forward/backward passes while reducing GPU memory usage further... placing weights in host memory actually reduces the required communication: They need to be sent from GPU to host during the first forward pass after each optimizer step, but the backward pass, and all subsequent forward passes for gradient accumulation, can use the values cached on the host.

claim: On a no-P2P PCIe fabric the correct ZeRO ordering is inverted: sharded model weights should be enabled BEFORE sharded gradients, contrary to traditional ZeRO levels, because host-cached weights remove the weight all-gather from the steady-state critical path.
stance_target: the default ZeRO-2/ZeRO-3 progression (gradients before weights) that FSDP-style implementations assume
scope_conditions: consumer GPUs, no PCIe P2P, FP8 weights gathered but BF16 gradients communicated
quoted_support: This also means that, contrary to traditional ZeRO levels, one should enable sharded model weights before enabling sharded gradients. This is especially true in FP8 training, when model weights are gathered in FP8 but gradients are communicated in BF16.

claim: NCCL all-gather and reduce-scatter collectives achieve quite low PCIe link utilization on consumer GPUs, whereas cudaMemcpy transfers driven by the GPU copy engines achieve much better utilization and do not reserve any SMs for communication kernels.
stance_target: the repo's measured ~0.75 GiB/s NCCL all-reduce and its claim that NCCL's SM-resident kernels are the wrong mechanism on this fabric
scope_conditions: 4x RTX 4090 workstation, PCIe 4.0, no P2P; all-gather and reduce-scatter for ZeRO-style training
quoted_support: When running all-gather (fetching model weights) and reduce-scatter (accumulating gradients) colletives with nccl, we observed that the PCIe link utilization was quite low. On the other hand, memory transfers handled by the GPUs copy-engines, as initiated by cudaMemcpy, do achieve much better utilization, and do not require reserving any SMs for communication kernels.

claim: The hardware gap between a datacenter GPU and a consumer GPU is 6x in BF16 TFLOPS (989.4 vs 165.2), 3.3x in memory (80 vs 24 GB), 3.3x in memory bandwidth (3.3 vs 1 TB/s), and 14x in interconnect bandwidth (900 GB/s NVLink vs 64 GB/s PCIe 4.0).
stance_target: the repo's premise that the box has A100-class matmul rates but a fabric an order of magnitude worse than a datacenter node
scope_conditions: H100 SXM vs RTX 4090; nominal specifications
quoted_support: Table 4: Comparison between datacentre and gaming GPUs. H100 / RTX 4090 / Ratio: BF16 [TFLOP/s] 989.4 / 165.2 / 6x; Memory [GB] 80 / 24 / 3.3x; Bandwidth [TB/s] 3.3 / 1 / 3.3x; Communication NVLink / PCIe 4.0; Bandwidth [GB/s] 900 / 64 / 14.

claim: A 7B model trained with full offloading needs about 54 GB of host memory: roughly 3 x 14 GB for optimizer state, 7 GB for quantized weights, and 5 GB for offloaded residuals.
stance_target: the host-RAM budget any offloaded 7B experiment on this box must reserve
scope_conditions: 7B model, 8-bit optimizer states, offloaded gradients and residuals
quoted_support: A 7B model needs approximately 3 x 14GB for the optimizer state, another 7GB for the quantized weights, and 5GB for offloaded residuals, a total of 54GB of memory.

claim: Zero-copy host-memory access gave poor PCIe bandwidth utilization on gaming GPUs (RTX 5060Ti, RTX 4090) but worked well on the higher-end L40S, while explicit double-buffering showed the reverse pattern, so the offload mechanism must be benchmarked per card rather than assumed.
stance_target: whether zero-copy or explicit double-buffering is the right offload path on an unusual card like the CMP 170HX
scope_conditions: RTX 5060Ti, RTX 4090, L40S; optimizer-state offload to pinned host memory
quoted_support: Interestingly, we found that zero-copy gave bad performance (i.e., low utilization of PCIe bandwidth) on gaming GPUs (5060Ti, 4090 but worked well on the more high-end cards (L40s), whereas the situation was reversed for double-buffering. Consequently, we recommend testing both options an the system in question and picking the faster one.

claim: LLMQ always shards optimizer states (ZeRO-1) in multi-GPU setups and allows model weights and gradients to be sharded independently, giving a continuum of memory/communication trade-offs rather than fixed ZeRO levels.
stance_target: what parallelism knobs an experiment on this box should expose
quoted_support: In a multi-GPU setup, LLMQ always shards optimizer states (ZeRO-1), and allows for sharding of model weights and gradients, independently.

claim: FP8 training yields about a 50% speed-up for sufficiently large models, but the benefit comes from faster GEMMs rather than from a larger batch size enabled by lower activation memory.
stance_target: whether low precision is a throughput lever worth testing on this box
scope_conditions: 3B-32B models; FP8 requires Ada (RTX 40xx) or Blackwell (RTX 50xx) for dynamic tensor-level scaling
quoted_support: The relative speed-up due to lower precision is shown in the SP column, and reaches about 50% for sufficiently large models... significant benefits from FP8 generally do not come from enabling a larger batch size due to lower activation memory requirements.
